CHAPTER 26 - COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS

Introduction

Communication is the process of transmitting information (voice, text, pictures, data) from one point to another. Modern life depends on electronic communication - radio, television, telephony, the internet, satellite links and mobile phones. This chapter describes how such systems work: the three basic building blocks of every communication system, the terminology used to describe signals, why signals must be 'modulated' before transmission, the main types of modulation (AM, FM and phase modulation), how radio waves travel from a transmitting antenna to a receiving antenna, and a brief look at satellite, optical-fibre and mobile communication.

26.1 ELEMENTS OF A COMMUNICATION SYSTEM

Every communication system, however simple or complex, has THREE essential parts:

(1) TRANSMITTER - it processes the information (the message) coming from a source and converts it into a form suitable for transmission over the channel. A transmitter typically contains a transducer (to convert sound or light into an electrical signal), a modulator (to impress the message on a high-frequency carrier), amplifiers and an antenna.

(2) COMMUNICATION CHANNEL (or medium) - the physical path over which the signal travels from transmitter to receiver. The channel may be a pair of wires, a coaxial cable, an optical fibre, or free space (for wireless/radio links). Every channel introduces some noise and attenuation.

(3) RECEIVER - it picks up the transmitted signal (which is now weak and mixed with noise), amplifies it, separates the message from the carrier (demodulation) and delivers it to the user through an output transducer such as a loudspeaker or a screen.

The simplest way to represent this is a BLOCK DIAGRAM:

  Information source -> Transmitter -> Channel -> Receiver -> User (destination)

The information source produces the message signal. The transmitter converts it to a transmitted signal. The channel carries it (adding noise). The receiver recovers the message. The destination is the person or device that finally uses the information.

26.2 BASIC TERMINOLOGY

SIGNAL: an electrical form of the message (a voltage or current that varies with time and carries information).

NOISE: unwanted, random electrical disturbances that mix with the signal in the channel and the receiver. Noise degrades the quality of communication. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) measures how strong the signal is compared with the noise.

ATTENUATION: the loss of strength (amplitude/power) of a signal as it travels through the channel. Attenuation increases with distance.

AMPLIFICATION: the process of increasing the amplitude/power of a signal using an electronic amplifier. It is needed at the transmitter (to boost the signal before sending) and at the receiver (to strengthen the weak received signal).

RANGE: the largest distance between transmitter and receiver up to which the signal can be received with acceptable strength and quality.

REPEATER: a combination of a receiver and a transmitter placed between the source and the destination. It picks up the weak/attenuated signal, amplifies (and reshapes) it, and retransmits it. Repeaters extend the range of communication. A communication satellite acts as a repeater in the sky.

BANDWIDTH: the range of frequencies (the difference between the highest and lowest frequency) present in a signal, or the range a channel can carry. Bandwidth = (highest frequency) - (lowest frequency). It is measured in hertz (Hz), kHz, MHz or GHz.

TRANSDUCER: a device that converts one form of energy into another (e.g. a microphone converts sound into an electrical signal; a loudspeaker does the reverse).

26.3 ANALOG AND DIGITAL SIGNALS

An ANALOG signal varies CONTINUOUSLY with time and can take any value within a range - for example the voltage produced by a microphone when someone speaks. A sine wave is the simplest analog signal.

A DIGITAL signal takes only a few DISCRETE values (usually two: 0 and 1, or LOW and HIGH). Computers, CDs and modern communication use digital signals because they are less affected by noise and can be regenerated exactly by repeaters. An analog signal is converted to digital form by sampling and coding (analog-to-digital conversion).

26.4 BANDWIDTH OF SIGNALS AND OF MEDIA

Different messages need different bandwidths:
 - Speech / telephone-quality audio: about 300 Hz to 3100 Hz, so a bandwidth of roughly 2800 Hz (about 3 kHz).
 - Music (high fidelity): about 20 Hz to 20 kHz, so a bandwidth of about 20 kHz.
 - Video (TV picture) signals: a bandwidth of about 4.2 MHz (a TV channel is allotted about 6 MHz to carry picture plus sound).

Transmission media also have limited bandwidths (their frequency-carrying capacity):
 - Two-wire lines and coaxial cables: up to a few hundred MHz.
 - Free space (radio links): the usable bandwidth depends on the frequency band and the antenna.
 - Optical fibre: enormously large bandwidth (many GHz to THz) because it uses light of very high frequency; this is why optical fibre carries huge amounts of data.

A channel must have a bandwidth at least as large as the bandwidth of the signal it is to carry.

26.5 THE NEED FOR MODULATION

The message signals (speech, music) are LOW-FREQUENCY (audio) signals, also called baseband signals. They cannot be transmitted efficiently over long distances directly. MODULATION is the process of superimposing the low-frequency message (modulating signal) on a high-frequency wave called the CARRIER. There are three main reasons why modulation is necessary:

(a) SIZE OF THE ANTENNA. For efficient radiation, the antenna length should be comparable to the wavelength of the signal - at least about lambda/4 (a quarter wavelength). Since wavelength lambda = c / f, a low audio frequency (say 15 kHz) has an enormous wavelength (c/f = 3x10^8 / 15000 = 20000 m), needing an antenna kilometres long - impossibly large. A high carrier frequency (say 1 MHz) has a wavelength of only 300 m, so the antenna becomes a few tens of metres - practical.

(b) EFFECTIVE POWER RADIATED / RANGE. The power radiated by an antenna is proportional to (length/wavelength)^2. A short antenna at low frequency radiates very little power; raising the frequency (by using a high-frequency carrier) increases the radiated power and hence the range.

(c) AVOIDING MIXING OF SIGNALS. If everyone transmitted their audio (baseband) signals directly, all signals (all in the same low band, say 0-20 kHz) would overlap and interfere - it would be impossible to separate one station from another. By modulating each message onto a DIFFERENT carrier frequency, many stations can share the same medium without interfering; the receiver simply tunes to the desired carrier.

26.6 TYPES OF MODULATION

A sinusoidal carrier is described by c(t) = A_c sin(2 pi f_c t + phi), where A_c is the amplitude, f_c the frequency and phi the phase. Modulation means varying one of these three quantities in step with the message signal. This gives three types:

(1) AMPLITUDE MODULATION (AM): the AMPLITUDE of the carrier is varied in proportion to the instantaneous value of the message signal, while the carrier frequency and phase stay constant.

(2) FREQUENCY MODULATION (FM): the FREQUENCY of the carrier is varied in proportion to the message signal, while the amplitude stays constant.

(3) PHASE MODULATION (PM): the PHASE of the carrier is varied in proportion to the message signal. FM and PM are closely related and are together called angle modulation.

MODULATION INDEX (for AM). For amplitude modulation, the modulation index (or modulation factor) is
   m = A_m / A_c
where A_m is the amplitude of the modulating (message) signal and A_c is the amplitude of the carrier. In terms of the maximum and minimum amplitudes of the modulated wave,
   m = (A_max - A_min) / (A_max + A_min).
The value of m lies between 0 and 1 (0 to 100%). If m > 1 the wave is OVER-MODULATED and the message gets distorted. Ideally m is kept close to 1 (but not more) for maximum undistorted power in the sidebands.

An AM wave contains the carrier frequency f_c and two SIDEBANDS at (f_c + f_m) and (f_c - f_m), where f_m is the message frequency. The bandwidth of an AM wave is therefore 2 f_m (twice the highest message frequency).

COMPARISON OF AM AND FM. FM is more immune to noise than AM (because noise mainly affects amplitude, and FM carries information in frequency, not amplitude); FM gives better sound quality but needs a larger bandwidth. AM has a smaller bandwidth and a larger range (AM broadcast can travel far via the ionosphere) but poorer quality. AM is used for medium-wave/short-wave broadcasting; FM for high-quality local radio and TV sound.

26.7 DEMODULATION (DETECTION)

At the receiver, the original message must be recovered from the modulated carrier. This reverse process is called DEMODULATION or DETECTION. For AM, a simple diode detector (a rectifier followed by a filter) recovers the audio signal; for FM, a frequency discriminator or ratio detector is used. After demodulation the audio is amplified and fed to the loudspeaker.

26.8 PROPAGATION OF ELECTROMAGNETIC (RADIO) WAVES

Radio waves radiated by a transmitting antenna reach the receiving antenna by three modes:

(a) GROUND (SURFACE) WAVE PROPAGATION. The wave travels along the surface of the Earth, following its curvature, guided by the ground. Ground-wave propagation works well only at LOW and MEDIUM frequencies (up to about 2 MHz) because higher-frequency waves are absorbed quickly by the ground. It is used for local AM (medium-wave) broadcasting. The range is limited (a few hundred km) as the wave is attenuated by the Earth.

(b) SKY WAVE (IONOSPHERIC) PROPAGATION. Waves in the frequency range of about 2 MHz to 30 MHz (short waves / HF) directed upward are REFLECTED (actually refracted back) by the IONOSPHERE - the layer of the upper atmosphere (about 60 km to 400 km altitude) ionised by solar radiation. By repeated reflections between the ionosphere and the Earth, short-wave signals travel very long distances (thousands of km) around the globe. This is used for long-distance and international short-wave broadcasting.
   The CRITICAL FREQUENCY (f_c) is the highest frequency that is reflected straight back by a given ionospheric layer when the wave is sent vertically upward. Waves of frequency higher than the critical frequency (above about 30 MHz) penetrate the ionosphere and escape into space instead of being reflected - so they cannot be used for sky-wave communication.

(c) SPACE WAVE (LINE-OF-SIGHT) PROPAGATION. At frequencies above about 30-40 MHz (VHF, UHF, microwaves), the wave travels in a straight line directly from the transmitting antenna to the receiving antenna (line-of-sight), or via a satellite. Because the Earth is curved, line-of-sight range is limited by the height of the antenna. For an antenna of height h on the Earth (radius R), the distance to the horizon is
   d = sqrt(2 R h).
Two tall antennas of heights h_T and h_R can communicate up to about d = sqrt(2 R h_T) + sqrt(2 R h_R). To cover large distances at these frequencies, tall towers, relay/repeater stations, or communication satellites are used. TV broadcasting, FM radio, radar, mobile phones and satellite links all use space-wave (line-of-sight) propagation.

26.9 THE ELECTROMAGNETIC SPECTRUM AND COMMUNICATION BANDS

Communication uses a wide range of frequencies. Some named bands:
 - MF (Medium Frequency, 300 kHz-3 MHz): AM (medium-wave) broadcast - ground wave.
 - HF (High Frequency, 3-30 MHz): short-wave broadcast - sky wave.
 - VHF (Very High Frequency, 30-300 MHz): FM radio, TV - space wave.
 - UHF (Ultra High Frequency, 300 MHz-3 GHz): TV, mobile phones, radar.
 - Microwaves (1 GHz and above): satellite links, radar, point-to-point relays.
 - Light (optical, ~10^14 Hz): optical-fibre communication.

26.10 SATELLITE, OPTICAL FIBRE AND MOBILE COMMUNICATION

SATELLITE COMMUNICATION. A communication satellite in a GEOSTATIONARY orbit (about 36000 km above the equator, period 24 hours, so it appears fixed in the sky) acts as a REPEATER. A ground station beams a microwave signal up to the satellite (the UPLINK); the satellite's transponder amplifies it and changes its frequency and beams it back to Earth (the DOWNLINK) to another ground station. Three geostationary satellites spaced 120 degrees apart can cover almost the whole globe. Satellites provide long-distance telephony, television relay, internet and weather/remote-sensing services.

OPTICAL FIBRE COMMUNICATION. An optical fibre is a very thin, flexible strand of glass (or plastic) that guides light by TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION along its length. Information is carried as pulses of laser/LED light. Because light has an extremely high frequency, optical fibre offers a HUGE bandwidth (very high data rate), very low loss (signals travel tens of km between repeaters), immunity from electrical interference, light weight and security. It forms the backbone of modern telephone and internet networks.

MOBILE (CELLULAR) TELEPHONY. A mobile-phone network divides a service area into small regions called CELLS, each served by a low-power base station (tower). Each cell uses a set of frequencies (UHF band, space-wave/line-of-sight); the same frequencies are re-used in distant, non-adjacent cells. As a moving user passes from one cell to the next, the call is automatically 'handed over' to the next base station without interruption. Base stations connect through a mobile switching centre to the wider telephone network. Cellular design allows a limited band of frequencies to serve millions of users at once.

SUMMARY

- A communication system has three parts: transmitter, channel (medium) and receiver; the block diagram is source -> transmitter -> channel -> receiver -> destination.
- Key terms: signal, noise, attenuation, amplification, range, bandwidth, repeater, transducer.
- Signals may be analog (continuous) or digital (discrete 0/1); digital resists noise better.
- Typical bandwidths: speech ~3 kHz, music ~20 kHz, video ~4.2 MHz. Optical fibre offers the largest channel bandwidth.
- Modulation (impressing the message on a high-frequency carrier) is needed to keep the antenna size practical, to radiate enough power/range, and to let many signals share the medium without mixing.
- Three modulation types: AM (vary amplitude), FM (vary frequency), PM (vary phase). For AM, modulation index m = A_m/A_c = (A_max - A_min)/(A_max + A_min), and 0 <= m <= 1; AM bandwidth = 2 f_m. FM is more noise-immune but needs more bandwidth. Demodulation recovers the message at the receiver.
- Radio waves propagate as ground (surface) waves (up to ~2 MHz), sky waves (2-30 MHz, reflected by the ionosphere; limited by the critical frequency), and space (line-of-sight) waves (above ~30 MHz). Line-of-sight range d = sqrt(2 R h).
- Satellite communication uses a geostationary satellite as a repeater (uplink/downlink). Optical fibre carries light by total internal reflection, giving huge bandwidth. Mobile telephony uses a cellular layout with frequency re-use and handover.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Communication Systems (NIOS Senior Secondary Physics)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Take the radius of the Earth R = 6.4 x 10^6 m and the speed of light c = 3 x 10^8 m/s where needed. Show your working for numerical problems.

questions.question: Draw (describe in words) the block diagram of a general communication system and name its three essential parts.
questions.answer:
Block diagram: Information source -> TRANSMITTER -> Communication CHANNEL (medium) -> RECEIVER -> Destination (user).
The three essential parts are:
(1) Transmitter - processes the message and converts it (by modulation and amplification) into a signal suitable for the channel, then radiates it through an antenna.
(2) Communication channel (medium) - the physical path (wire, cable, optical fibre or free space) that carries the signal; it adds noise and attenuation.
(3) Receiver - picks up the weak signal, amplifies it, demodulates it to recover the message, and delivers it to the user through an output transducer.
questions.explanation: The three-block model (Tx-channel-Rx) with source and destination at the ends.

questions.question: Define bandwidth. State the approximate bandwidths required for (a) speech, (b) music and (c) a TV video signal.
questions.answer:
Bandwidth is the range of frequencies present in a signal (or that a channel can carry): bandwidth = highest frequency - lowest frequency, measured in Hz/kHz/MHz.
(a) Speech (telephone quality): about 300 Hz to 3100 Hz, i.e. a bandwidth of about 2800 Hz (~3 kHz).
(b) Music (high fidelity): about 20 Hz to 20 kHz, i.e. a bandwidth of about 20 kHz.
(c) TV video signal: about 4.2 MHz (a full TV channel is allotted about 6 MHz).
questions.explanation: Definition plus the three standard bandwidth figures.

questions.question: Explain why modulation is necessary before transmitting an audio message. Give the three main reasons with reasoning.
questions.answer:
Audio (baseband) signals are low-frequency (20 Hz to 20 kHz) and cannot be transmitted efficiently on their own. Modulation impresses them on a high-frequency carrier. Three reasons:
(1) ANTENNA SIZE. An antenna radiates efficiently only if its length is about lambda/4 or more. Since lambda = c/f, an audio frequency of 15 kHz gives lambda = 3x10^8 / 15000 = 20000 m, needing an antenna about 5 km long - impractical. A 1 MHz carrier gives lambda = 300 m, so an antenna of a few tens of metres works.
(2) POWER RADIATED / RANGE. The power radiated by an antenna is proportional to (length/lambda)^2. Low-frequency signals have huge lambda, so a practical antenna radiates almost no power. A high-frequency carrier makes length/lambda large enough to radiate useful power and give good range.
(3) AVOIDING MIXING OF SIGNALS. If all stations sent their audio directly they would all occupy the same 0-20 kHz band and interfere. Modulating each message onto a DIFFERENT carrier frequency separates the stations; the receiver tunes to the wanted carrier. Thus modulation makes antennas practical, boosts range, and lets many channels share the medium.
questions.explanation: Antenna size (lambda/4), radiated power (length/lambda)^2, and frequency-division to avoid mixing.

questions.question: A carrier of amplitude 10 V is amplitude-modulated by a signal of amplitude 6 V. Find the modulation index. Is the wave over-modulated?
questions.answer:
Modulation index m = A_m / A_c = 6 / 10 = 0.6 (i.e. 60%).
Since m = 0.6 is less than 1, the wave is NOT over-modulated - it is properly modulated with no distortion. (Over-modulation occurs only when m > 1.)

questions.question: An AM wave has maximum amplitude 15 V and minimum amplitude 5 V. Calculate its modulation index.
questions.answer:
Using m = (A_max - A_min) / (A_max + A_min):
m = (15 - 5) / (15 + 5) = 10 / 20 = 0.5 (i.e. 50%).
The wave is properly modulated (m = 0.5 < 1).
questions.explanation: m = (A_max-A_min)/(A_max+A_min) = 10/20 = 0.5.

questions.question: A TV tower has a height of 80 m. Taking the radius of the Earth as 6.4 x 10^6 m, find the line-of-sight range of transmission.
questions.answer:
Line-of-sight (space-wave) range d = sqrt(2 R h).
Here R = 6.4 x 10^6 m and h = 80 m.
d = sqrt(2 x 6.4 x 10^6 x 80) = sqrt(1.024 x 10^9) = 3.2 x 10^4 m = 32 km (approximately).
So the tower can transmit up to about 32 km to a receiver at ground level.
questions.explanation: d = sqrt(2 R h) = sqrt(2 x 6.4e6 x 80) = sqrt(1.024e9) ~ 3.2e4 m = 32 km.

questions.question: Describe the three modes of propagation of radio waves. For each, give the frequency range and one use.
questions.answer:
(1) GROUND (SURFACE) WAVE: the wave travels along the Earth's surface following its curvature, guided by the ground. Effective only at low/medium frequencies up to about 2 MHz (higher frequencies are absorbed by the ground). Range is a few hundred km. Use: medium-wave (AM) local broadcasting.
(2) SKY WAVE: waves of about 2 MHz to 30 MHz sent upward are reflected (refracted) back by the IONOSPHERE (60-400 km up). By repeated reflections between ionosphere and Earth the wave travels thousands of km. The CRITICAL FREQUENCY is the highest frequency reflected straight back; above about 30 MHz waves penetrate the ionosphere and escape. Use: long-distance/international short-wave broadcasting.
(3) SPACE (LINE-OF-SIGHT) WAVE: at frequencies above about 30-40 MHz (VHF/UHF/microwave) the wave travels in a straight line from transmitting to receiving antenna, or via a satellite. Range is limited by antenna height, d = sqrt(2 R h). Use: TV, FM radio, radar, mobile phones, satellite links.
questions.explanation: Ground (<2 MHz), sky (2-30 MHz, ionosphere), space (>30 MHz, line-of-sight) with uses.

questions.question: How does a geostationary satellite act as a repeater in satellite communication? Mention uplink and downlink.
questions.answer: A geostationary satellite orbits about 36000 km above the equator with a 24-hour period, so it appears fixed in the sky. It carries a transponder that acts as a REPEATER: a ground station beams a microwave signal up to the satellite (the UPLINK); the transponder receives this weak signal, amplifies it and shifts it to a different frequency, then beams it back to Earth (the DOWNLINK) to another ground station. Because it is high above the Earth, one satellite covers a huge area; three such satellites 120 degrees apart can cover almost the whole globe for telephony, TV relay and internet.
questions.explanation: Geostationary orbit; transponder amplifies and re-transmits; uplink up, downlink down.

questions.question: State two advantages of optical-fibre communication over communication using metallic wires.
questions.answer:
Advantages of optical fibre over metallic wire:
(1) Very LARGE BANDWIDTH - because it uses light of very high frequency, an optical fibre can carry an enormous amount of information (very high data rate).
(2) Very LOW LOSS - signals travel tens of km before needing a repeater, and there is no electromagnetic interference/cross-talk. (Also: light weight, cheaper raw material (silica), and more secure.)
questions.explanation: Huge bandwidth and low loss/immunity to interference are the key gains.

questions.question: Distinguish between analog and digital signals, and state one reason digital signals are preferred in modern communication.
questions.answer:
An ANALOG signal varies CONTINUOUSLY with time and can take any value in a range (e.g. the voltage from a microphone). A DIGITAL signal takes only a few DISCRETE values, usually two - 0 and 1 (LOW and HIGH).
Digital signals are preferred because they are much less affected by noise: a repeater can regenerate a clean 0/1 pattern exactly, whereas noise added to an analog signal cannot be fully removed. Digital form also allows compression, encryption and error correction.

questions.question: Name the three essential parts of any communication system.
questions.answer: The three essential parts are: (1) the TRANSMITTER (processes and sends the signal), (2) the COMMUNICATION CHANNEL or medium (carries the signal), and (3) the RECEIVER (recovers the message for the user).
questions.explanation: Transmitter, channel, receiver.

questions.question: What is a transducer? Give one example each of an input and an output transducer used in communication.
questions.answer: A transducer is a device that converts one form of energy into another. In communication it converts between the physical message and an electrical signal. Input transducer example: a MICROPHONE, which converts sound (pressure waves) into an electrical signal. Output transducer example: a LOUDSPEAKER, which converts an electrical signal back into sound. (A TV camera and a screen are another such pair for video.)
questions.explanation: Definition plus microphone (input) and loudspeaker (output).

questions.question: State the function of a repeater and give an everyday example.
questions.answer: A repeater is a combination of a receiver and a transmitter placed along the transmission path. It picks up the weak, attenuated signal, amplifies (and reshapes) it, and retransmits it, thereby extending the range of communication. Example: a communication satellite acts as a repeater in the sky; relay towers along a microwave link are also repeaters.
questions.explanation: Amplifies and retransmits to extend range; satellite is an example.

questions.question: Define noise and attenuation.
questions.answer: NOISE is the unwanted, random electrical disturbance that mixes with the signal in the channel and receiver and degrades the quality of communication. ATTENUATION is the loss of strength (amplitude/power) of a signal as it travels through the channel; it increases with distance.
questions.explanation: Noise = random unwanted disturbance; attenuation = loss of strength with distance.

questions.question: Distinguish between analog and digital signals with one example of each.
questions.answer: An ANALOG signal varies continuously with time and can take any value within a range - for example the voltage produced by a microphone during speech, or a sine wave. A DIGITAL signal takes only a few discrete values, usually two (0 and 1 / LOW and HIGH) - for example the bit-stream inside a computer or on a CD. Digital signals resist noise better and can be regenerated exactly by a repeater.
questions.explanation: Continuous (microphone voltage) vs discrete 0/1 (computer data).

questions.question: What is meant by the bandwidth of a signal? How is it calculated?
questions.answer: The bandwidth of a signal is the range of frequencies present in it. It is calculated as the difference between the highest and the lowest frequency in the signal: bandwidth = f_highest - f_lowest. It is measured in Hz, kHz, MHz or GHz. A channel must have at least this much bandwidth to carry the signal faithfully.
questions.explanation: Range of frequencies = highest minus lowest.

questions.question: Why are digital signals less affected by noise than analog signals?
questions.answer: A digital signal has only two levels (0 and 1). When noise is added, the level is still clearly closer to 0 or to 1, so a regenerator/repeater can decide which was sent and rebuild a clean, exact copy - the noise is removed. An analog signal can take any value, so noise added to it becomes part of the waveform and cannot be separated out; each repeater amplifies both signal and noise. Hence digital transmission preserves quality over long distances far better.
questions.explanation: Two-level signals can be regenerated exactly; analog noise cannot be removed.

questions.question: State the approximate bandwidths of a speech signal and a music signal.
questions.answer: Speech (telephone quality): frequencies about 300 Hz to 3100 Hz, giving a bandwidth of about 2800 Hz (~3 kHz). Music (high fidelity): frequencies about 20 Hz to 20 kHz, giving a bandwidth of about 20 kHz.
questions.explanation: Speech ~3 kHz, music ~20 kHz.

questions.question: A video signal occupies frequencies from 0 to 4.2 MHz. What is its bandwidth, and why does video need much more bandwidth than speech?
questions.answer: The bandwidth is 4.2 MHz - 0 = 4.2 MHz. Video needs far more bandwidth than speech because a picture carries a very large amount of information per second (many lines and picture elements changing rapidly, 25-30 frames per second), whereas speech is a single slowly-varying sound of limited frequency range (~3 kHz). More information per second means more frequency components, hence a larger bandwidth.
questions.explanation: 4.2 MHz; a picture carries far more information per second than speech.

questions.question: Why does optical fibre offer a much larger bandwidth than a metallic wire?
questions.answer: An optical fibre carries information as light, whose frequency is enormously high (~10^14 Hz), whereas a metallic wire carries electrical signals at radio frequencies (up to a few hundred MHz). Since a larger carrier frequency can accommodate a much wider band of modulating frequencies, the fibre can carry far more information (much higher data rate) - a very large bandwidth. Fibre also has very low loss and no electrical interference.
questions.explanation: Light's very high frequency allows a very wide modulation band.

questions.question: Define modulation and name the wave on which the message is superimposed.
questions.answer: Modulation is the process of superimposing a low-frequency message (modulating) signal on a high-frequency wave so that it can be transmitted efficiently over long distances. The high-frequency wave on which the message is impressed is called the CARRIER.
questions.explanation: Impressing the message on a high-frequency carrier.

questions.question: An audio signal of 20 kHz is to be radiated directly. Calculate the wavelength and the minimum antenna length (lambda/4), and comment.
questions.answer: Wavelength lambda = c/f = (3 x 10^8) / (20 x 10^3) = 1.5 x 10^4 m = 15000 m. Minimum antenna length ~ lambda/4 = 15000/4 = 3750 m = 3.75 km. Such an antenna (nearly 4 km tall) is impossible to build. This is why the audio must instead be modulated onto a high-frequency carrier, which has a short wavelength and hence a practical antenna length.
questions.explanation: lambda = 15000 m, lambda/4 = 3.75 km - impractical, so modulation is needed.

questions.question: Give the three reasons why modulation is necessary.
questions.answer: (1) ANTENNA SIZE: efficient radiation needs an antenna of length about lambda/4; low audio frequencies have huge wavelengths requiring kilometre-long antennas, so a high-frequency carrier is used to shorten the antenna to a practical size. (2) RADIATED POWER/RANGE: radiated power is proportional to (length/lambda)^2, so a high carrier frequency lets a practical antenna radiate enough power for good range. (3) AVOIDING MIXING OF SIGNALS: putting each message on a different carrier frequency lets many stations share the medium without interfering; the receiver tunes to the desired carrier.
questions.explanation: Antenna size, radiated power/range, and avoiding mixing of signals.

questions.question: A carrier of amplitude 8 V is amplitude-modulated by a 2 V signal. Find the modulation index and state whether it is over-modulated.
questions.answer: Modulation index m = A_m/A_c = 2/8 = 0.25 (25%). Since m = 0.25 is less than 1, the wave is NOT over-modulated; it is properly (under-)modulated with no distortion.
questions.explanation: m = 2/8 = 0.25 < 1, not over-modulated.

questions.question: An AM wave has A_max = 16 V and A_min = 4 V. Find (a) the modulation index and (b) the carrier and signal amplitudes.
questions.answer:
(a) m = (A_max - A_min)/(A_max + A_min) = (16 - 4)/(16 + 4) = 12/20 = 0.6 (60%).
(b) Carrier amplitude A_c = (A_max + A_min)/2 = (16 + 4)/2 = 10 V. Signal amplitude A_m = (A_max - A_min)/2 = (16 - 4)/2 = 6 V. Check: m = A_m/A_c = 6/10 = 0.6, consistent.

questions.question: A 1000 kHz carrier is amplitude-modulated by a 5 kHz tone. Find the sideband frequencies and the bandwidth of the AM wave.
questions.answer: Sidebands are at f_c +/- f_m: upper = 1000 + 5 = 1005 kHz; lower = 1000 - 5 = 995 kHz. Bandwidth = 2 f_m = 2 x 5 = 10 kHz (from 995 kHz to 1005 kHz).
questions.explanation: Sidebands 995 and 1005 kHz; bandwidth 10 kHz.

questions.question: Name the three types of modulation and state which property of the carrier each varies.
questions.answer: (1) Amplitude modulation (AM) - varies the AMPLITUDE of the carrier. (2) Frequency modulation (FM) - varies the FREQUENCY of the carrier. (3) Phase modulation (PM) - varies the PHASE of the carrier. FM and PM together are called angle modulation.
questions.explanation: AM-amplitude, FM-frequency, PM-phase.

questions.question: Compare AM and FM with respect to noise immunity, bandwidth and sound quality.
questions.answer: NOISE: FM is more immune to noise than AM, because most noise adds to the amplitude of a wave, and FM carries its information in the frequency (not the amplitude), so amplitude noise can be limited/clipped off at the receiver. BANDWIDTH: FM needs a LARGER bandwidth than AM (AM bandwidth = 2 f_m; FM is wider). QUALITY: FM gives better, clearer sound quality; AM has poorer quality but a smaller bandwidth and greater range. Hence AM is used for long-range medium/short-wave broadcasting and FM for high-quality local radio and TV sound.
questions.explanation: FM: more noise-immune, wider bandwidth, better quality; AM: narrower band, longer range.

questions.question: Describe sky-wave propagation and explain the role of the critical frequency.
questions.answer: In sky-wave propagation, radio waves of about 2-30 MHz directed upward are reflected (refracted) back to Earth by the IONOSPHERE, the ionised upper atmosphere (60-400 km high). By repeated reflections between the ionosphere and the ground, short waves reach thousands of km, giving long-distance/international broadcasting. The CRITICAL FREQUENCY is the highest frequency that the ionosphere reflects straight back for a vertically incident wave. Waves of frequency greater than the critical frequency (above about 30 MHz) are not reflected - they penetrate the ionosphere and escape into space, so they cannot be used for sky-wave communication.
questions.explanation: Ionospheric reflection of 2-30 MHz; above f_critical the wave escapes.

questions.question: A transmitting antenna is 125 m tall. Taking R = 6.4 x 10^6 m, find its line-of-sight range.
questions.answer: Line-of-sight range d = sqrt(2 R h) = sqrt(2 x 6.4 x 10^6 x 125) = sqrt(1.6 x 10^9) = 4.0 x 10^4 m = 40 km (approximately). So the antenna covers about 40 km to a receiver at ground level.

questions.question: Explain briefly how a cellular mobile telephone network works.
questions.answer: A cellular network divides the service area into small regions called CELLS, each served by a low-power base station (tower) using a set of UHF frequencies (space-wave/line-of-sight). The same frequencies are RE-USED in distant, non-adjacent cells, so a limited band of frequencies can serve very many users. As a moving user crosses from one cell into the next, the call is automatically HANDED OVER to the new base station without interruption. Base stations link through a mobile switching centre to the rest of the telephone network.
questions.explanation: Cells with base stations, frequency re-use, and handover between cells.

questions.question: State two advantages of optical-fibre communication.
questions.answer: (1) Very LARGE BANDWIDTH: because it uses light of very high frequency, an optical fibre can carry an enormous amount of information (very high data rate). (2) Very LOW LOSS and immunity to electrical interference: signals travel tens of km between repeaters with no cross-talk. (Also light weight, security, and cheap raw material.)
questions.explanation: Huge bandwidth and low loss/interference immunity.

questions.question: With the help of a block diagram, describe the function of each part of a communication system.
questions.answer:
Block diagram: Information source -> TRANSMITTER -> Communication CHANNEL -> RECEIVER -> Destination.
(1) INFORMATION SOURCE: produces the message (voice, text, picture, data).
(2) TRANSMITTER: converts the message into a signal suitable for the channel. It contains an input transducer (e.g. microphone), a modulator that impresses the message on a high-frequency carrier, amplifiers, and a transmitting antenna that radiates the signal.
(3) COMMUNICATION CHANNEL (medium): the physical path - wire, cable, optical fibre or free space - along which the signal travels. Every channel introduces noise and attenuation, weakening and corrupting the signal.
(4) RECEIVER: picks up the weak, noisy signal through a receiving antenna, amplifies it, and demodulates (detects) it to recover the original message, which is then delivered through an output transducer (loudspeaker/screen).
(5) DESTINATION: the person or device that finally uses the information. Repeaters/amplifiers may be placed along the channel to extend the range.
questions.explanation: Source, transmitter (transducer+modulator+antenna), channel, receiver (demodulator), destination.

questions.question: Explain, with calculations, why an audio signal cannot be transmitted directly but must be modulated onto a carrier.
questions.answer:
An audio signal has low frequency (20 Hz to 20 kHz). Consider the reasons:
(1) ANTENNA SIZE. Efficient radiation needs an antenna of length about lambda/4, where lambda = c/f. For f = 15 kHz, lambda = 3x10^8 / 15000 = 20000 m, so lambda/4 = 5000 m - a 5 km antenna is impossible. If instead the audio modulates a 1 MHz carrier, lambda = 3x10^8 / 10^6 = 300 m and lambda/4 = 75 m - a practical antenna.
(2) RADIATED POWER/RANGE. The power radiated by an antenna is proportional to (length/lambda)^2. At audio frequencies lambda is huge, so any practical antenna radiates almost no power and the range is negligible. A high-frequency carrier makes length/lambda large, so useful power is radiated and the range increases.
(3) MIXING OF SIGNALS. All audio signals lie in the same 0-20 kHz band; if transmitted directly they would overlap and interfere hopelessly. By modulating each onto a DIFFERENT carrier frequency, many stations coexist and the receiver tunes to the wanted one.
Hence modulation is essential: it gives a practical antenna, adequate radiated power/range, and separation of channels.
questions.explanation: Antenna lambda/4 calculation, radiated power (l/lambda)^2, and channel separation.

questions.question: Define modulation index for AM and derive m = (A_max - A_min)/(A_max + A_min). A carrier of 50 V is modulated to 60% - find A_m, A_max and A_min.
questions.answer:
For AM the carrier amplitude is varied by the message. The modulation index m = A_m/A_c, where A_m is the message amplitude and A_c the carrier amplitude.
The envelope of the AM wave has maximum and minimum amplitudes:
  A_max = A_c + A_m (carrier plus signal add)
  A_min = A_c - A_m (carrier minus signal)
Adding: A_max + A_min = 2 A_c. Subtracting: A_max - A_min = 2 A_m.
Dividing: (A_max - A_min)/(A_max + A_min) = 2 A_m / 2 A_c = A_m/A_c = m. Hence m = (A_max - A_min)/(A_max + A_min).

Numerical: A_c = 50 V, m = 0.60.
 A_m = m x A_c = 0.60 x 50 = 30 V.
 A_max = A_c + A_m = 50 + 30 = 80 V.
 A_min = A_c - A_m = 50 - 30 = 20 V.
Check: (80 - 20)/(80 + 20) = 60/100 = 0.6. Correct.
questions.explanation: Derivation from A_max=A_c+A_m, A_min=A_c-A_m; then A_m=30 V, A_max=80 V, A_min=20 V.

questions.question: Describe amplitude modulation and frequency modulation. What are sidebands, and what is the bandwidth of an AM wave?
questions.answer:
A sinusoidal carrier is c(t) = A_c sin(2 pi f_c t + phi). Modulation varies one of its three quantities:
AMPLITUDE MODULATION (AM): the amplitude A_c is made to vary in proportion to the instantaneous message value, while f_c and phi stay constant. The 'envelope' of the wave then follows the message shape.
FREQUENCY MODULATION (FM): the frequency f_c is varied in proportion to the message, while the amplitude stays constant. Louder sound = larger frequency swing. FM is more immune to noise but uses a wider bandwidth.
SIDEBANDS: when a carrier f_c is amplitude-modulated by a message of frequency f_m, the AM wave contains three frequencies - the carrier f_c, an upper sideband at (f_c + f_m) and a lower sideband at (f_c - f_m). The message information is carried in the sidebands.
BANDWIDTH of AM: it is the difference between the highest and lowest frequencies present = (f_c + f_m) - (f_c - f_m) = 2 f_m, i.e. twice the highest modulating frequency.
questions.explanation: AM varies amplitude, FM varies frequency; sidebands at f_c +/- f_m; AM bandwidth = 2 f_m.

questions.question: Explain the three modes by which radio waves travel from the transmitting to the receiving antenna, giving frequency ranges.
questions.answer:
(1) GROUND (SURFACE) WAVE: the wave travels along the Earth's surface, following its curvature and guided by the ground. It works well only at low and medium frequencies up to about 2 MHz, since higher frequencies are strongly absorbed by the ground. Range is limited to a few hundred km. Used for medium-wave (AM) broadcasting.
(2) SKY WAVE: waves of about 2-30 MHz sent upward are reflected back by the IONOSPHERE (60-400 km up). Repeated reflections between ionosphere and Earth carry the signal thousands of km. The critical frequency limits this - waves above ~30 MHz penetrate the ionosphere and escape. Used for long-distance short-wave broadcasting.
(3) SPACE (LINE-OF-SIGHT) WAVE: at frequencies above about 30-40 MHz (VHF/UHF/microwave) the wave travels in a straight line directly from transmitter to receiver, or via a satellite. Because the Earth curves away, the range is limited by antenna height: d = sqrt(2 R h). Tall towers, relay stations or satellites extend the coverage. Used for TV, FM radio, radar, mobile phones and satellite links.
questions.explanation: Ground (<2 MHz), sky (2-30 MHz, ionosphere), space (>30 MHz, line-of-sight, d=sqrt(2Rh)).

questions.question: A transmitting antenna of height 80 m and a receiving antenna of height 20 m are used (R = 6.4 x 10^6 m). Find the maximum line-of-sight distance between them.
questions.answer:
For two antennas the maximum line-of-sight distance is d = sqrt(2 R h_T) + sqrt(2 R h_R).
For the transmitting antenna (h_T = 80 m): sqrt(2 x 6.4x10^6 x 80) = sqrt(1.024x10^9) = 3.2 x 10^4 m = 32 km.
For the receiving antenna (h_R = 20 m): sqrt(2 x 6.4x10^6 x 20) = sqrt(2.56x10^8) = 1.6 x 10^4 m = 16 km.
Total d = 32 + 16 = 48 km.
So the two antennas can communicate over a maximum line-of-sight distance of about 48 km.
questions.explanation: d = sqrt(2Rh_T)+sqrt(2Rh_R) = 32 + 16 = 48 km.

questions.question: Describe satellite communication. Explain the terms geostationary orbit, transponder, uplink and downlink.
questions.answer: In satellite communication, a communication satellite in space acts as a REPEATER between two ground stations. A GEOSTATIONARY ORBIT is a circular orbit about 36000 km above the equator with a period of 24 hours; the satellite revolves in step with the Earth's rotation and so appears fixed in the sky, allowing ground antennas to point at it permanently. The satellite carries a TRANSPONDER - a receiver-amplifier-transmitter unit. A ground station beams a microwave signal up to the satellite: this is the UPLINK. The transponder receives the weak signal, amplifies it and shifts it to a different frequency, then re-transmits it back to Earth: this is the DOWNLINK, received by another ground station. Because the satellite is very high, one satellite covers a huge area; three geostationary satellites spaced 120 degrees apart cover almost the whole globe. Satellites provide long-distance telephony, TV relay, internet and weather/remote-sensing services.
questions.explanation: Geostationary (~36000 km, 24 h); transponder repeater; uplink up, downlink down.

questions.question: Explain the following terms used in communication: signal, noise, attenuation, amplification, range and bandwidth.
questions.answer:
SIGNAL: the electrical form of the message - a voltage or current that varies with time and carries the information.
NOISE: unwanted, random electrical disturbance that mixes with the signal in the channel and receiver and degrades the quality of communication; it is measured relative to the signal by the signal-to-noise ratio.
ATTENUATION: the loss of strength (amplitude/power) of a signal as it travels through the channel; it increases with distance, which is why long links need boosting.
AMPLIFICATION: the process of increasing the amplitude/power of a signal using an electronic amplifier; used at the transmitter before sending and at the receiver to strengthen the weak received signal.
RANGE: the largest distance between transmitter and receiver over which the signal can be received with acceptable strength and quality.
BANDWIDTH: the range of frequencies present in a signal, or that a channel can carry; bandwidth = highest frequency - lowest frequency, measured in Hz/kHz/MHz.
questions.explanation: Definitions of the six basic communication terms.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Every communication system, from a simple intercom to a satellite TV link, can be represented by a block diagram in which the message flows from a source, through a transmitter, a channel and a receiver, to a destination.

(i) Name the three essential parts of the system.
(ii) In which part does modulation take place?
(iii) In which part does demodulation take place?
(iv) What does the channel add to the signal?
questions.answer:
(i) The transmitter, the communication channel (medium), and the receiver.
(ii) Modulation takes place in the TRANSMITTER.
(iii) Demodulation takes place in the RECEIVER.
(iv) The channel adds NOISE and causes ATTENUATION (loss of strength) of the signal.
questions.explanation: Three parts; modulation at Tx, demodulation at Rx; channel adds noise/attenuation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A signal weakens as it travels along a channel and picks up random disturbances on the way. To send it far, engineers place devices along the route that restore the signal.

(i) What is the weakening of the signal called?
(ii) What are the random disturbances called?
(iii) Name the device that restores and retransmits the signal.
(iv) Why is a digital signal easier to restore than an analog one?
questions.answer:
(i) Weakening of the signal is called ATTENUATION.
(ii) The random disturbances are called NOISE.
(iii) The device is a REPEATER (a receiver + transmitter that amplifies and retransmits).
(iv) A digital signal has only two levels (0 and 1); even with noise the level is clearly closer to 0 or 1, so it can be regenerated exactly. An analog signal can take any value, so noise mixed into it cannot be separated out.
questions.explanation: Attenuation, noise, repeater; digital regenerated exactly.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Different messages need different bandwidths: speech about 3 kHz, hi-fi music about 20 kHz and a TV video signal about 4.2 MHz. Media differ too - optical fibre offers by far the largest bandwidth.

(i) What is meant by bandwidth?
(ii) Which of the three messages needs the largest bandwidth and why?
(iii) A speech channel is 300 Hz to 3300 Hz. What is its bandwidth?
(iv) Why does optical fibre have such a large bandwidth?
questions.answer:
(i) Bandwidth is the range of frequencies present in a signal (or that a channel can carry) = highest frequency - lowest frequency.
(ii) The TV VIDEO signal (~4.2 MHz), because a picture carries far more information per second (many picture elements changing rapidly) than speech or music.
(iii) 3300 - 300 = 3000 Hz (3 kHz).
(iv) Optical fibre carries light of very high frequency (~10^14 Hz), which can accommodate a very wide band of modulating frequencies, giving a huge bandwidth (very high data rate).
questions.explanation: Definition; video largest; 3000 Hz; fibre uses high-frequency light.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

An audio signal of 15 kHz cannot be radiated directly because the antenna needed would be several kilometres long. Instead the audio is impressed on a high-frequency carrier.

(i) What is this process called?
(ii) Find the wavelength of a 15 kHz signal (c = 3 x 10^8 m/s).
(iii) Estimate the minimum antenna length (lambda/4) for it.
(iv) Give one more reason (besides antenna size) why modulation is needed.
questions.answer:
(i) The process is called MODULATION.
(ii) lambda = c/f = 3 x 10^8 / 15000 = 20000 m (20 km).
(iii) Minimum antenna length ~ lambda/4 = 20000/4 = 5000 m (5 km) - impractical.
(iv) Other reasons: modulation increases the power radiated (and hence the range), and it lets many stations share the medium on different carrier frequencies without their signals mixing.
questions.explanation: Modulation; lambda = 20 km; lambda/4 = 5 km; also range and avoiding mixing.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

An amplitude-modulated wave is observed on an oscilloscope. Its maximum amplitude is 18 V and its minimum amplitude is 6 V.

(i) Write the formula for modulation index in terms of A_max and A_min.
(ii) Calculate the modulation index.
(iii) Find the carrier and modulating-signal amplitudes.
(iv) Is the wave over-modulated?
questions.answer:
(i) m = (A_max - A_min) / (A_max + A_min).
(ii) m = (18 - 6)/(18 + 6) = 12/24 = 0.5 (50%).
(iii) A_c = (A_max + A_min)/2 = (18 + 6)/2 = 12 V; A_m = (A_max - A_min)/2 = (18 - 6)/2 = 6 V. Check m = 6/12 = 0.5.
(iv) No - since m = 0.5 is less than 1, the wave is properly modulated, not over-modulated.
questions.explanation: m = 0.5; A_c = 12 V, A_m = 6 V; not over-modulated.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A broadcast station uses a carrier of frequency 800 kHz. It transmits speech containing frequencies up to 4 kHz using amplitude modulation.

(i) At what frequencies do the two sidebands appear?
(ii) What is the bandwidth of this AM signal?
(iii) If the carrier amplitude is 100 V and the modulation index is 0.7, find the modulating signal amplitude.
(iv) State what happens if the modulation index exceeds 1.
questions.answer:
(i) Sidebands at f_c +/- f_m = 800 +/- 4 = 796 kHz (lower) and 804 kHz (upper).
(ii) Bandwidth = 2 f_m = 2 x 4 = 8 kHz.
(iii) A_m = m x A_c = 0.7 x 100 = 70 V.
(iv) If m > 1 the wave is over-modulated: the envelope gets clipped/distorted and the recovered message is distorted, so m is kept at or below 1.
questions.explanation: Sidebands 796/804 kHz; bandwidth 8 kHz; A_m = 70 V; m>1 distorts.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Two radio stations broadcast the same programme - one in the AM medium-wave band and one in the FM band. Listeners report that the FM broadcast sounds clearer and has less background hiss, but it can only be heard within the city.

(i) In AM and FM, which property of the carrier is varied in each?
(ii) Why is the FM broadcast less affected by noise?
(iii) Why does FM need a larger bandwidth than AM?
(iv) Why can the FM signal be heard only within the city while AM travels farther?
questions.answer:
(i) AM varies the AMPLITUDE of the carrier; FM varies its FREQUENCY.
(ii) Most noise adds to the AMPLITUDE of a wave. Since FM carries its information in the frequency, amplitude noise can be limited/removed at the receiver, so FM is quieter.
(iii) FM conveys information through frequency variations that produce many sidebands spread over a wider frequency range, so it occupies a larger bandwidth than AM (whose bandwidth is only 2 f_m).
(iv) FM uses high (VHF) frequencies that travel as space (line-of-sight) waves, limited to the horizon, so coverage is local. AM medium-wave travels as ground and sky waves (reflected by the ionosphere), reaching much farther.
questions.explanation: AM-amplitude/FM-frequency; noise is amplitude-based; FM wider band; FM line-of-sight vs AM ground/sky wave.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A television transmitting tower is 90 m high. Television is broadcast in the VHF/UHF band. (Take R = 6.4 x 10^6 m.)

(i) By which mode do VHF/UHF waves travel?
(ii) Write the formula for line-of-sight range.
(iii) Calculate the range of this tower.
(iv) Suggest one way to increase the coverage area.
questions.answer:
(i) VHF/UHF waves travel as SPACE (line-of-sight) waves.
(ii) Line-of-sight range d = sqrt(2 R h).
(iii) d = sqrt(2 x 6.4x10^6 x 90) = sqrt(1.152x10^9) = 3.39 x 10^4 m ~ 34 km.
(iv) Increase the coverage by using a taller tower, or by adding relay/repeater stations, or by using a satellite (all extend the limited line-of-sight range).
questions.explanation: Space wave; d = sqrt(2Rh) ~ 34 km; taller tower/relays/satellite.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Short-wave radio stations can be heard on other continents, thousands of kilometres away, even though the transmitter's line-of-sight range is only a few tens of kilometres.

(i) By which mode do these short waves travel such huge distances?
(ii) Which atmospheric layer makes this possible?
(iii) What is the critical frequency?
(iv) What happens to a wave whose frequency is above the critical frequency?
questions.answer:
(i) They travel by SKY-WAVE propagation.
(ii) The IONOSPHERE (the ionised upper atmosphere, 60-400 km high) reflects the waves back to Earth.
(iii) The critical frequency is the highest frequency that the ionosphere reflects straight back for a vertically incident wave.
(iv) A wave of frequency above the critical frequency is not reflected - it penetrates the ionosphere and escapes into outer space, so it cannot be used for sky-wave communication.
questions.explanation: Sky wave; ionosphere; critical frequency; higher frequencies escape.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A satellite parked about 36000 km above the equator relays telephone and TV signals between distant ground stations. A ground station sends the signal up to it and another station receives it back.

(i) What name is given to this type of orbit?
(ii) Name the device on the satellite that receives, amplifies and re-transmits the signal.
(iii) Name the up-going and down-going links.
(iv) Roughly how many such satellites cover almost the whole Earth?
questions.answer:
(i) The orbit is a GEOSTATIONARY orbit (period 24 hours, so the satellite appears fixed in the sky).
(ii) The TRANSPONDER (it acts as a repeater).
(iii) The up-going link (ground to satellite) is the UPLINK; the down-going link (satellite to ground) is the DOWNLINK.
(iv) Three geostationary satellites, spaced 120 degrees apart, cover almost the entire globe.
questions.explanation: Geostationary; transponder; uplink/downlink; three satellites.
